paper_context.research_question: How can synsets be automatically induced from ambiguous synonymy graphs extracted from collaborative lexical resources, and can a graph-based approach combining word sense induction with global clustering outperform existing methods?
contribution_type: methodological framework for fuzzy graph clustering via hard clustering
empirical validation across multiple languages and gold standards
resource construction (induced synsets for English and Russian)
main_claims: A meta-algorithm combining local word sense induction with global hard clustering can effectively perform fuzzy clustering of synonym graphs
Disambiguating the input graph by splitting polysemous nodes reduces problematic hub effects that link semantically unrelated nodes
WATSET outperforms five state-of-the-art methods (Chinese Whispers, MCL, MaxMax, ECO, CPM) in F-score on four gold standard datasets (WordNet, BabelNet, RuThes, YARN)
Word embedding-based edge weighting (cosine similarity) is superior to binary or frequency-based weighting across methods
The approach requires no pivot English resource, unlike BabelNet/UBY, and avoids error-prone mapping and machine translation procedures
Results are robust across resource-rich (English) and under-resourced (Russian) languages
expected_evaluation_dimensions: F-score, precision, and recall on gold standard synset datasets
Comparative performance against five baseline graph clustering algorithms
Impact of edge weighting schemes (ones, count, sim) on method performance
Cross-dataset evaluation and generalization across languages
Sensitivity to input dictionary completeness and sparseness
Granularity analysis of induced synsets (number of synsets, cluster sizes)
Qualitative analysis of synset quality and meaningfulness
Computational efficiency and scalability (implicit in algorithm design)

extracted_claims.claim_text: A meta-algorithm combining local word sense induction with global hard clustering can effectively perform fuzzy clustering of synonym graphs
evidence: Our meta-clustering approach lets us use an efficient hard clustering algorithm to perform fuzzy clustering of the graph
The method consists of five steps: (1) learning word embeddings; (2) constructing the ambiguous weighted graph; (3) inducing word senses; (4) constructing disambiguated graph; (5) global clustering
uncertainty_flags: No theoretical proof of optimality or convergence properties provided
Effectiveness demonstrated empirically but mechanism of why hard clustering on disambiguated graph achieves fuzzy clustering not formally justified
Sensitivity to hyperparameters (e.g., cluster size threshold of 150 words) not systematically analyzed

extracted_claims.claim_label: Hub effect reduction via node disambiguation
extracted_claims.claim_text: Disambiguating the input graph by splitting polysemous nodes reduces problematic hub effects that link semantically unrelated nodes
evidence: The disambiguation of the input graph performed by the WATSET method splits nodes belonging to several local communities to several nodes significantly facilitating the clustering task otherwise complicated by the presence of the hubs
Figure 2 illustrates how polysemous 'bank' is split into bank1, bank2, bank3, bank4 with distinct contexts
uncertainty_flags: No quantitative measurement of hub effect magnitude before/after disambiguation
Claim relies on intuitive explanation rather than graph-theoretic analysis
No ablation study isolating the contribution of disambiguation step alone

extracted_claims.claim_label: WATSET outperforms five baselines on F-score
extracted_claims.claim_text: WATSET outperforms five state-of-the-art methods (Chinese Whispers, MCL, MaxMax, ECO, CPM) in F-score on four gold standard datasets (WordNet, BabelNet, RuThes, YARN)
evidence: Table 3: WATSET[MCL, MCL] achieves F-score 0.331 on WordNet vs MCL 0.321, CWnolog 0.304, MaxMax 0.192, ECO 0.136, CPMk=2 0.234
Table 3: WATSET[MCL, MCL] achieves F-score 0.374 on BabelNet vs MCL 0.369, CWnolog 0.350, MaxMax 0.228, ECO 0.190, CPMk=2 0.332
Table 4: WATSET[CWlog, MCL] achieves F-score 0.139 on RuThes vs MCL 0.152, CWnolog 0.105, MaxMax 0.164, ECO 0.042, CPMk=3 0.075
Table 4: WATSET[CWlog, MCL] achieves F-score 0.428 on YARN vs MCL 0.423, CWnolog 0.402, MaxMax 0.327, ECO 0.004, CPMk=3 0.110
uncertainty_flags: RuThes results show WATSET does NOT outperform MCL (0.139 vs 0.152) and MaxMax (0.139 vs 0.164) in F-score
Claim overstates consistency: WATSET wins on 3 of 4 datasets, not all four
Absolute F-scores are low across all methods (max 0.428), raising questions about practical utility
Different WATSET configurations used for different datasets, complicating direct comparison

extracted_claims.claim_text: Word embedding-based edge weighting (cosine similarity) is superior to binary or frequency-based weighting across methods
extracted_claims.section_anchor: Section 5.1 (Impact of Graph Weighting Schema), Figure 3
evidence: Figure 3 shows sim weighting outperforms ones and count across most methods on both English datasets

Results across various configurations and methods indicate that using the weights based on the similarity scores provided by word embeddings is the best strategy for all the methods but MaxMax on both English datasets
uncertainty_flags: Claim qualified by exception: MaxMax performs better with ones weighting on some datasets
Russian datasets show less consistent pattern in Figure 3
No statistical significance testing provided
Mechanism of why embedding similarity improves clustering not explained

extracted_claims.claim_text: The approach requires no pivot English resource, unlike BabelNet/UBY, and avoids error-prone mapping and machine translation procedures
evidence: In contrast to the projects like BabelNet and UBY, which rely on English WordNet as a pivot for mapping of existing resources, our approach requires no such pivot lexical ontologies
The potential advantages of our approach as compared to BabelNet/UBY is the (1) absence of the error-prone procedures of mapping and machine translation
uncertainty_flags: Claim is architectural/design-based, not empirically validated
No direct comparison with BabelNet/UBY on same input data
Advantage of avoiding mapping errors not quantified
Requires word embeddings trained on language-specific corpora, which is a different dependency

extracted_claims.claim_text: Results are robust across resource-rich (English) and under-resourced (Russian) languages
evidence: Evaluation on two English datasets (WordNet, BabelNet) and two Russian datasets (RuThes, YARN)
WATSET shows competitive performance on both language groups
uncertainty_flags: Russian results show lower absolute F-scores (max 0.428 vs 0.374 for English), suggesting language-dependent performance
Only two languages tested; generalization to other under-resourced languages unclear
Russian input dictionary is larger (202K synonyms vs 71K for English), contradicting 'under-resourced' characterization
No analysis of what makes Russian 'under-resourced' or how method specifically addresses this

extracted_claims.claim_text: The toughest competitor was a hard clustering algorithm—MCL, which successfully groups monosemous words but produces nonsensical clusters when polysemous words appear
evidence: We observed that the 'plain' MCL successfully groups the monosemous words, but produces nonsensical clusters of moderate size, e.g., 20–50 words, when a polysemous word appears, resulting in the precision drop w.r.t. WATSET
uncertainty_flags: Characterization of MCL clusters as 'nonsensical' is qualitative, not quantified
No analysis of which specific polysemous words cause MCL to fail
No ablation study comparing MCL on monosemous vs polysemous subgraphs
Claim based on observation rather than systematic analysis

extracted_claims.claim_text: A limitation of all approaches considered in this paper is the dependence on completeness of the input dictionary of synonyms; missing bridges between words lead to smaller-than-desired synsets
evidence: In some parts of the input synonymy graph, important bridges between words can be missing, leading to smaller-than-desired synsets
Low performance on RuThes attributed to limited coverage of input dictionary on domain-specific vocabulary
uncertainty_flags: Limitation acknowledged but not systematically studied
No experiments with artificially degraded input dictionaries to quantify sensitivity
Proposed extension (using distributional models to enhance connectivity) not implemented or evaluated
Unclear how much of performance variance is due to dictionary completeness vs other factors

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Synsets are naturally represented as cliques in a synonymy graph where nodes are words and edges are synonymy relations
supporting_evidence: A synset is a set of mutual synonyms, which can be represented as a clique where nodes are words and edges are synonymy relations
The cliques in such a graph naturally form densely connected sets of synonyms corresponding to concepts
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If synsets do not form cliques (e.g., if some synonymy pairs are missing or if synonymy is not transitive), the graph clustering approach may fail to recover true synsets. This is partially acknowledged in the discussion of input dictionary completeness.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Word embeddings trained on large corpora provide reliable cosine similarity measures for weighting synonymy edges
identified_assumptions.section_anchor: Section 3.1 (Learning Word Embeddings), Section 3.2 (Construction of a Synonymy Graph)
supporting_evidence: We consider the distributional semantic similarity measures based on word embeddings as a possible edge weighing approach
Figure 3 shows sim weighting outperforms ones and count across methods
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If embeddings are poorly trained, noisy, or misaligned with synonymy relations, edge weights will be unreliable. The paper does not validate embedding quality or analyze failure cases where embedding similarity contradicts true synonymy.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Word sense induction via ego network clustering on the local neighborhood of a word can reliably identify distinct senses of that word
supporting_evidence: We use a graph-based word sense induction method that is similar to the curvature-based approach of Dorow and Widdows (2003)
Each cluster is hopefully representing a different sense of the word u
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If ego network clustering fails to separate senses (e.g., for words with subtle sense distinctions or rare senses), the subsequent disambiguation step will propagate errors. The word 'hopefully' signals uncertainty about this assumption.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Cosine similarity between sense contexts in vector space reliably disambiguates neighboring words to their correct senses
supporting_evidence: For recovering these sense labels of the neighbouring words, we employ the following sense disambiguation approach... we estimate the most similar sense of that word û using the cosine similarity measure
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If context vectors are noisy or if multiple senses have similar contexts, disambiguation will be incorrect, leading to spurious edges in the disambiguated graph G'. No evaluation of disambiguation accuracy is provided.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Hard clustering on the disambiguated graph G' produces valid fuzzy clustering of the original ambiguous graph G
supporting_evidence: Our meta-clustering approach lets us use an efficient hard clustering algorithm to perform fuzzy clustering of the graph
Running a hard clustering algorithm on G' produces the desired set of synsets
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the mapping from hard clusters on G' back to fuzzy clusters on G is not valid (e.g., if sense nodes from the same word are assigned to different clusters), the output synsets will be incorrect. No formal justification of this mapping is provided.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Pruning clusters larger than 150 words removes spurious giant components without removing valid synsets
supporting_evidence: During the evaluation, we delete the clusters equal or larger than the threshold of 150 words as they hardly can represent any meaningful synset
Without this pruning, the MaxMax and CPM methods tend to discover giant components obtaining almost zero precision
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If valid synsets contain more than 150 words (e.g., for highly polysemous words or broad concepts), they will be incorrectly removed. The threshold appears arbitrary and is not justified empirically.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Gold standard synsets from WordNet, BabelNet, RuThes, and YARN are sufficiently complete and accurate to serve as evaluation benchmarks
supporting_evidence: We use WordNet, a popular English lexical database crafted by a group of expert lexicographers
We use BabelNet, a large-scale multilingual semantic network constructed automatically
We use RuThes and YARN for Russian
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If gold standards are incomplete (missing valid synonymy pairs) or contain errors, F-score metrics will be misleading. The paper acknowledges that RuThes has limited coverage of domain-specific vocabulary and that YARN was filtered to synsets edited at least 8 times, introducing potential bias.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: F-score on binary synonymy pairs is an appropriate metric for evaluating synset quality
supporting_evidence: To evaluate the quality of the induced synsets, we transformed them into binary synonymy relations and computed precision, recall, and F-score on the basis of the overlap of these binary relations with the binary relations from the gold standard datasets
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: F-score on pairs does not capture synset granularity, cluster coherence, or semantic meaningfulness. Two synsets with identical pairwise overlaps may have very different quality. The paper notes granularity differences (3,729 to 61,126 synsets) but does not evaluate whether granularity is appropriate.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The same input synonymy dictionary can be used to evaluate against multiple gold standards without introducing bias
supporting_evidence: For Russian, the same input synonymy dictionary was used by authors of YARN to construct synsets using crowdsourcing. Therefore, results on the YARN dataset show how close an automatic synset induction method can approximate manually created synsets provided the same starting raw linguistic materials
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Using the same input dictionary for both method input and gold standard evaluation (YARN case) introduces circularity and inflates performance metrics. The paper acknowledges this but does not correct for it.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Chinese Whispers and Markov Clustering are suitable hard clustering algorithms for the global clustering step
supporting_evidence: In our experiments, we test Chinese Whispers and Markov Clustering
Different WATSET configurations use different combinations of algorithms for WSI and global clustering
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If these algorithms are not well-suited to the structure of the disambiguated graph, performance will be suboptimal. The paper does not justify why these specific algorithms were chosen or compare against other hard clustering methods.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper presents WATSET, a meta-algorithm for synset induction from ambiguous synonymy graphs. The core logical argument is: (1) synsets are cliques in synonymy graphs; (2) hard clustering alone fails on polysemous words due to hub effects; (3) local word sense induction (WSI) disambiguates nodes; (4) hard clustering on the disambiguated graph achieves fuzzy clustering. The paper demonstrates empirical outperformance on English datasets (WordNet, BabelNet) and YARN (Russian), with competitive results on RuThes. However, the logical chain exhibits critical weaknesses: the claim of outperformance on all four datasets is contradicted by RuThes results; the mechanism linking disambiguation to hub reduction lacks formal justification; and the evaluation methodology contains circularity (YARN uses the same input dictionary). The paper's strength lies in its clear methodological contribution and multi-lingual validation, but the reasoning breaks at the claim-to-evidence linkage for generalization across languages and the theoretical justification for why the approach works.
logical_argument_graph: Premise 1: Synsets are cliques in synonymy graphs (Section 1, 3)
Premise 2: Input synonymy graphs from collaborative resources are ambiguous (Section 1, 3.2)
Premise 3: Hard clustering algorithms (MCL, CW) fail on polysemous words due to hub effects (Section 3, 5.2)
Premise 4: Word sense induction via ego network clustering can separate word senses locally (Section 3.3)
Premise 5: Disambiguating neighbors via cosine similarity of sense contexts reduces hubs (Section 3.4)
Claim A: Hard clustering on disambiguated graph G' achieves fuzzy clustering of original graph G (Section 3.5)
Claim B: WATSET outperforms five baselines on F-score across all four datasets (Abstract, Section 5)
Claim C: Embedding-based edge weighting (sim) is superior to binary/frequency weighting (Section 5.1)
Claim D: The approach requires no English pivot resource, unlike BabelNet/UBY (Section 1, 2)
Claim E: Results are robust across resource-rich (English) and under-resourced (Russian) languages (Section 4, 5)
BREAK POINT 1: Claim B contradicted by RuThes data (Table 4: WATSET F=0.139 vs MCL F=0.152, MaxMax F=0.164)
BREAK POINT 2: Claim A lacks formal justification—no proof that hard clusters on G' map validly to fuzzy clusters on G

BREAK POINT 3: Claim E weakened by: (a) Russian input dictionary larger than English (202K vs 71K), contradicting 'under-resourced' framing; (b) lower absolute F-scores on Russian (max 0.428 vs 0.374 English); (c) only two languages tested
BREAK POINT 4: Claim C qualified by exceptions (MaxMax performs better with ones weighting; Russian datasets show inconsistent patterns)
BREAK POINT 5: Hub effect reduction (Premise 5) is intuitive but not quantified; no ablation study isolates this component's contribution
BREAK POINT 6: Circular evaluation on YARN (Premise 2 + Claim B): same input dictionary used for both method input and gold standard construction inflates performance metrics

Conclusion: WATSET shows competitive performance on English and YARN, but claims of universal outperformance and language robustness are overstated; theoretical mechanism of fuzzy clustering via hard clustering on disambiguated graph remains unjustified

strengths.title: Clear methodological contribution with intuitive design
strengths.description: The five-step WATSET pipeline is well-motivated and clearly presented. The core insight—that local WSI followed by global hard clustering can achieve fuzzy clustering—is novel and addresses a real limitation of existing hard clustering algorithms on polysemous words. The method is simple enough to be reproducible and implementable.
evidence: Section 3 provides clear step-by-step description with Figure 1 outline
Figure 2 effectively illustrates the disambiguation process with concrete example (bank)
Method avoids complex fuzzy clustering algorithms by leveraging simpler hard clustering on disambiguated graph

strengths.title: Comprehensive multi-lingual evaluation across multiple gold standards
strengths.description: The paper evaluates on four gold standard datasets across two languages (English: WordNet, BabelNet; Russian: RuThes, YARN), providing broader validation than single-dataset studies. This multi-lingual approach is valuable for demonstrating applicability beyond English.
evidence: Tables 1-2 provide detailed statistics of gold standards and input dictionaries
Section 4 systematically describes evaluation setup for both languages
Tables 3-4 show results across all four datasets with consistent methodology

strengths.title: Systematic comparison against five state-of-the-art baselines
strengths.description: The paper compares against a diverse set of baselines (Chinese Whispers, MCL, MaxMax, ECO, CPM) representing different clustering paradigms (hard, fuzzy, clique-based). This breadth of comparison strengthens the empirical validation.
evidence: Section 2 provides detailed descriptions of each baseline method
Tables 3-4 show WATSET against all five baselines with multiple metrics (precision, recall, F-score)
Section 5.2 provides qualitative analysis of why each baseline fails (hub effects, giant components, etc.)

strengths.title: Thorough analysis of edge weighting strategies
strengths.description: Section 5.1 systematically evaluates three edge weighting schemes (ones, count, sim) across all methods and datasets. This analysis provides practical guidance for practitioners and demonstrates that embedding-based weighting is generally superior.
evidence: Figure 3 visualizes impact of weighting schemes across methods and datasets
Text explains why sim weighting works better (distributional semantics aligns with synonymy)
Analysis identifies exception (MaxMax) and discusses implications

strengths.title: Practical resource contribution with implementation release
strengths.description: The paper releases induced synset resources for English and Russian, along with an implementation of WATSET. This makes the contribution immediately useful to the community and enables reproducibility.
evidence: Abstract mentions 'An implementation of the WATSET method is available online, along with induced lexical resources'
Section 4.4 provides detailed statistics of induced resources
Table 6 shows qualitative examples of induced synsets

strengths.title: Honest discussion of limitations and failure modes
strengths.description: Section 6 acknowledges key limitations (input dictionary completeness, cross-dataset performance variation, low absolute F-scores) and discusses why they occur. This transparency is valuable for understanding the method's scope.
evidence: Discussion of RuThes vs YARN performance difference (domain-specific vocabulary coverage)
Acknowledgment of circular evaluation on YARN (same input dictionary used for both method and gold standard)
Proposed extension using distributional models to enhance connectivity

concerns.title: Critical contradiction in main claim: RuThes results contradict outperformance claim
concerns.description: The abstract and Section 5 claim WATSET outperforms all five baselines on all four datasets. However, Table 4 shows WATSET[CWlog, MCL] achieves F-score 0.139 on RuThes, which is lower than MCL (0.152) and MaxMax (0.164). This directly contradicts the stated claim of outperformance on all four datasets.
evidence: Abstract: 'outperforms five state-of-the-art methods... in terms of F-score on four different gold standard datasets'
Section 5: 'WATSET robustly outperformed all other methods according to F-score on both English datasets (Table 3) and on the YARN dataset for Russian (Table 4)'
Table 4 RuThes row: WATSET[CWlog, MCL] F=0.139 vs MCL F=0.152, MaxMax F=0.164
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Revise abstract and Section 5 to accurately state that WATSET outperforms baselines on 3 of 4 datasets (WordNet, BabelNet, YARN) but not on RuThes. Provide analysis of why RuThes is different (domain-specific vocabulary, input dictionary coverage) and discuss whether this represents a fundamental limitation or a tuning issue.

concerns.title: Lack of formal justification for fuzzy clustering via hard clustering on disambiguated graph
concerns.description: The core claim (C1) that hard clustering on G' produces valid fuzzy clustering of G lacks formal justification. The paper does not prove that the mapping from hard clusters on sense nodes back to fuzzy clusters on original words is valid or that this approach is theoretically sound.
evidence: Section 3.5: 'As the result, running a hard clustering algorithm on G′ produces the desired set of synsets' (stated as fact without proof)
No formal definition of how hard clusters on V' (sense nodes) map to fuzzy clusters on V (original words)
No analysis of whether sense nodes from the same word can be assigned to different clusters (which would violate fuzzy clustering semantics)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide formal definition of the mapping from hard clusters on G' to fuzzy clusters on G. Prove or empirically validate that this mapping preserves the fuzzy clustering property. Alternatively, clarify that the output is not truly fuzzy clustering but rather a hard clustering of sense nodes that can be interpreted as fuzzy clustering of words.

concerns.title: Hub effect reduction mechanism not quantified or validated
concerns.description: Claim C2 asserts that disambiguation reduces hub effects, but this is not quantified. No metrics measure hub effect magnitude before/after disambiguation, and no ablation study isolates the contribution of the disambiguation step.
evidence: Section 5.2: 'The disambiguation of the input graph performed by the WATSET method splits nodes belonging to several local communities to several nodes significantly facilitating the clustering task otherwise complicated by the presence of the hubs' (qualitative assertion)
Figure 2 shows single example but no systematic analysis
No ablation study comparing WATSET with/without disambiguation step
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Quantify hub effects using graph-theoretic measures (e.g., degree distribution, clustering coefficient, number of nodes with degree > threshold). Measure these before/after disambiguation. Conduct ablation study comparing WATSET with a variant that skips the disambiguation step. Analyze which specific polysemous words cause MCL to fail and how disambiguation helps.

concerns.title: Circular evaluation on YARN: same input dictionary used for both method and gold standard
concerns.description: Section 4.4 states: 'Note that the same input synonymy dictionary was used by authors of YARN to construct synsets using crowdsourcing.' This creates circularity: the method is evaluated against a gold standard constructed from the same input data, inflating performance metrics and making YARN results not directly comparable to other datasets.
evidence: Section 4.4: 'the same input synonymy dictionary was used by authors of YARN to construct synsets using crowdsourcing'
Table 4: YARN shows highest F-score (0.428) compared to RuThes (0.139), suggesting input dictionary alignment matters
Discussion acknowledges this but does not correct for it in results
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clearly flag YARN results as not directly comparable to other datasets due to circular evaluation. Consider reporting YARN results separately or with a caveat. Alternatively, evaluate on a held-out subset of YARN not used in the input dictionary, or use a different Russian gold standard without this circularity.

concerns.title: Arbitrary cluster size threshold of 150 words not empirically justified
concerns.description: Section 5 states: 'During the evaluation, we delete the clusters equal or larger than the threshold of 150 words as they hardly can represent any meaningful synset.' This threshold appears arbitrary and is not empirically justified. No sensitivity analysis shows how results vary with different thresholds.
evidence: Section 5: 'we delete the clusters equal or larger than the threshold of 150 words'
No justification for why 150 is chosen
No sensitivity analysis showing impact of different thresholds
Section 5.2: 'Without this pruning, the MaxMax and CPM methods tend to discover giant components obtaining almost zero precision' (suggests threshold is method-dependent)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide empirical justification for the 150-word threshold. Conduct sensitivity analysis showing F-score as a function of threshold for all methods. Consider using method-specific thresholds if different methods require different pruning strategies. Alternatively, use a principled approach (e.g., based on gold standard synset size distribution) to set the threshold.

concerns.title: Different WATSET configurations used for different datasets complicates interpretation
concerns.description: Tables 3-4 show different WATSET configurations for different datasets: WATSET[MCL, MCL] for English, WATSET[CWlog, MCL] for Russian. This makes it unclear which design choices matter and whether the method is robust to configuration choices.
evidence: Table 3: WATSET[MCL, MCL] used for English datasets
Table 4: WATSET[CWlog, MCL] used for Russian datasets
Section 5.2 explains why: 'Using CW instead of MCL for word sense induction in WATSET expectedly produces fine-grained senses... these senses erroneously tend to form coarse-grained synsets'
No systematic analysis of which configuration is optimal for which dataset
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report results for all WATSET configurations on all datasets to show robustness. Provide principled guidance for selecting configurations based on dataset characteristics. Alternatively, identify a single configuration that works well across all datasets and use it consistently.

concerns.title: No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals for performance comparisons
concerns.description: Tables 3-4 report point estimates of F-score without statistical significance tests or confidence intervals. Given low absolute F-scores (max 0.428) and small differences between methods (e.g., WATSET 0.374 vs MCL 0.369 on BabelNet), it is unclear whether differences are statistically significant.
evidence: Tables 3-4 report only point estimates
No confidence intervals or p-values provided
BabelNet: WATSET[MCL, MCL] F=0.374 vs MCL F=0.369 (difference of 0.005)
YARN: WATSET[CWlog, MCL] F=0.428 vs MCL F=0.423 (difference of 0.005)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct statistical significance tests (e.g., bootstrap resampling, permutation tests) to determine whether performance differences are significant. Report 95% confidence intervals for all metrics. Discuss practical significance of observed differences given low absolute F-scores.

concerns.title: Word sense induction step uses uncertain language ('hopefully') without validation
concerns.description: Section 3.3 states: 'each cluster is hopefully representing a different sense of the word u'. This indicates uncertainty about whether ego network clustering reliably separates word senses. No evaluation of WSI accuracy is provided.
evidence: Section 3.3: 'each cluster is hopefully representing a different sense of the word u'
No evaluation of WSI accuracy (e.g., comparison against gold standard word senses)
No analysis of failure cases where ego network clustering fails to separate senses
No ablation study showing impact of WSI quality on final synset quality
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate WSI accuracy on a subset of words with known senses (e.g., from WordNet). Analyze failure cases where ego network clustering fails to separate senses. Conduct ablation study showing how WSI errors propagate to final synsets. Consider alternative WSI methods if ego network clustering is unreliable.

concerns.title: Disambiguation accuracy not evaluated; errors could propagate to final synsets
concerns.description: Section 3.4 describes the disambiguation step but does not evaluate its accuracy. If disambiguation is incorrect (e.g., if cosine similarity between sense contexts is noisy), errors will propagate to the final synsets.
evidence: Section 3.4: 'we estimate the most similar sense of that word û using the cosine similarity measure' (no validation of accuracy)
No evaluation of disambiguation accuracy against gold standard sense assignments
No analysis of when disambiguation fails (e.g., for words with similar sense contexts)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate disambiguation accuracy on a subset of words with known sense assignments. Analyze failure cases where cosine similarity between sense contexts is misleading. Conduct ablation study showing impact of disambiguation errors on final synset quality. Consider alternative disambiguation methods if cosine similarity is unreliable.

concerns.title: Low absolute F-scores across all methods raise questions about task difficulty and evaluation setup
concerns.description: Maximum F-score across all methods and datasets is 0.428 (WATSET on YARN). Such low scores raise questions about whether the task is well-defined, whether evaluation metrics are appropriate, or whether the gold standards are too strict.
evidence: Table 3: Max F-score 0.374 (WATSET on BabelNet)
Table 4: Max F-score 0.428 (WATSET on YARN), 0.152 (MCL on RuThes)

Section 6: 'While the results obtained for the English datasets are in agreement (Tables 3 and 5), the results measured on RuThes and YARN datasets for Russian show a similar global picture in terms of relevant ranking of the methods, yet absolute scores are largely different'
No discussion of whether F-score on binary pairs is appropriate metric for synset quality
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze why F-scores are low. Is it due to: (a) incomplete gold standards (missing valid synonymy pairs)? (b) inappropriate evaluation metric (F-score on pairs doesn't capture synset quality)? (c) inherent difficulty of the task? Conduct error analysis on a sample of induced synsets to understand failure modes. Consider alternative evaluation metrics (e.g., synset granularity, cluster coherence, semantic meaningfulness).

concerns.title: Cross-linguistic robustness claim weakened by language-dependent performance and limited language coverage
concerns.description: Claim C6 asserts robustness across resource-rich and under-resourced languages, but evidence is weak: (a) Russian input dictionary is larger than English (202K vs 71K), contradicting 'under-resourced' framing; (b) Russian F-scores are lower (max 0.428 vs 0.374 English), suggesting language-dependent degradation; (c) only two languages tested, limiting generalization.
evidence: Section 4: 'Russian is a good example of an under-resourced language'
Table 2: Russian input dictionary has 202K synonyms vs 71K for English
Table 4: RuThes F=0.139 (much lower than English datasets)
Only English and Russian tested; no evaluation on other under-resourced languages
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify what 'under-resourced' means in this context. If it refers to lack of manually-constructed lexical resources (not input dictionary size), state this explicitly. Analyze why Russian performance is lower despite larger input dictionary. Test on additional under-resourced languages (e.g., Polish, Turkish, Hindi) to validate cross-linguistic robustness claim.

concerns.title: Embedding-based edge weighting superiority claim not validated for Russian
concerns.description: Claim C4 asserts that embedding-based weighting (sim) is superior across methods, but Figure 3 shows inconsistent patterns for Russian datasets. The claim is primarily supported by English results.
evidence: Section 5.1: 'using the weights based on the similarity scores provided by word embeddings is the best strategy for all the methods but MaxMax on both English datasets'
Figure 3: Russian datasets (RuThes, YARN) show less clear superiority of sim weighting
No explicit analysis of Russian weighting results
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze Figure 3 results for Russian datasets explicitly. If sim weighting is not consistently superior for Russian, revise claim to specify that it applies primarily to English. Investigate why embedding quality or alignment with synonymy might differ between languages.

concerns.title: Input dictionary completeness limitation acknowledged but not systematically studied
concerns.description: Claim C8 acknowledges that input dictionary completeness affects performance, but this is not systematically studied. No experiments with artificially degraded dictionaries quantify sensitivity, and the proposed extension (using distributional models) is not implemented.
evidence: Section 6: 'one limitation of all approaches considered in this paper is the dependence on completeness of the input dictionary of synonyms'
No sensitivity analysis with degraded input dictionaries
Proposed extension 'using the distributional models to enhance connectivity of the graph' not implemented or evaluated
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct sensitivity analysis by artificially removing edges from the input dictionary and measuring impact on F-score. Implement and evaluate the proposed extension using distributional models to enhance connectivity. Analyze which types of missing edges (e.g., rare synonyms, domain-specific terms) have the largest impact on performance.

concerns.title: No ablation study isolating contributions of individual components
concerns.description: The paper does not provide ablation studies isolating the contributions of individual components (WSI, disambiguation, global clustering). This makes it difficult to assess which components drive performance improvements.
evidence: No variant of WATSET without WSI step
No variant without disambiguation step
No comparison of different WSI algorithms (only CW and MCL tested)
No comparison of different global clustering algorithms beyond CW and MCL
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct ablation studies: (1) WATSET without WSI (direct hard clustering on G); (2) WATSET without disambiguation (hard clustering on G with sense nodes but without disambiguating neighbors); (3) WATSET with alternative WSI algorithms; (4) WATSET with alternative global clustering algorithms. Report F-scores for each variant to quantify component contributions.

concerns.title: Embedding quality and alignment with synonymy not validated
concerns.description: The method relies on word embeddings for both edge weighting and sense context representation, but embedding quality and alignment with synonymy relations are not validated.
evidence: Section 4.3: Embeddings trained on Google News (English) and lib.rus.ec (Russian) but no validation of quality
Section 3.2: 'sim that assigns every edge (u, v) a weight equal to the cosine similarity of the skip-gram word vectors' (assumes embeddings align with synonymy)
No analysis of cases where embedding similarity contradicts true synonymy
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Validate embedding quality using standard benchmarks (e.g., word similarity tasks, analogy tasks). Analyze correlation between embedding cosine similarity and gold standard synonymy relations. Identify cases where embeddings fail to capture synonymy and discuss implications for the method.

uncertainty_flags: RuThes results directly contradict main claim of outperformance on all four datasets—this is a critical factual error that undermines the paper's central contribution

Cluster size threshold of 150 words appears arbitrary and is not empirically justified
Input dictionary completeness limitation acknowledged but not systematically studied
No ablation studies isolating contributions of individual components (WSI, disambiguation, global clustering)
alternative_interpretations: The RuThes results could indicate that WATSET is optimized for English-like language structures or for resources with high input dictionary coverage, rather than being universally robust. The method may require language-specific tuning.

Low absolute F-scores across all methods could indicate that the task is inherently difficult (e.g., due to incomplete gold standards or ambiguous synonymy definitions) rather than a flaw in the methods. The ranking of methods may be more meaningful than absolute scores.

The hub effect reduction could be achieved not by the disambiguation step itself, but by the combination of WSI + global clustering, which naturally produces finer-grained senses. The specific mechanism of improvement may differ from the paper's explanation.

The superiority of embedding-based weighting could reflect the quality of the specific embeddings used (Google News for English, lib.rus.ec for Russian) rather than a general principle. Different embeddings might show different patterns.

The circular evaluation on YARN could be viewed as a strength rather than a weakness: it shows how close automatic induction can get to manual construction when using the same input materials. However, this should be clearly labeled as a different evaluation scenario.

The different WATSET configurations for different datasets could indicate that the method is flexible and can be tuned to dataset characteristics, rather than a weakness. However, this requires principled guidance for configuration selection.
transparency_notes: The paper's main claim (outperformance on all four datasets) is contradicted by the RuThes results presented in Table 4. This appears to be a factual error rather than a matter of interpretation.
The paper acknowledges circular evaluation on YARN but does not correct for it in the results or discussion. YARN results should be interpreted differently from other datasets.

The paper uses different WATSET configurations for different datasets without explaining why or providing principled guidance for configuration selection. This limits reproducibility and generalization.

The paper's characterization of Russian as 'under-resourced' is inconsistent with the fact that the Russian input dictionary (202K synonyms) is larger than the English input dictionary (71K synonyms). The term 'under-resourced' likely refers to lack of manually-constructed lexical resources, not input dictionary size.
The paper's claim of 'robustness' across languages is weakened by the fact that Russian F-scores are substantially lower than English F-scores, suggesting language-dependent performance degradation.
The paper does not provide statistical significance tests or confidence intervals, making it unclear whether observed performance differences are meaningful given the low absolute F-scores.

The paper's discussion of why MCL is the 'toughest competitor' does not explain why MCL outperforms WATSET on RuThes, which contradicts the narrative that WATSET's disambiguation solves MCL's hub problem.
The paper's proposed extension (using distributional models to enhance connectivity) is mentioned but not implemented or evaluated, limiting the practical impact of the acknowledged limitation.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The WATSET meta-algorithm combining local WSI with global hard clustering to achieve fuzzy clustering is novel and lacks close analogs in the retrieved literature. The approach is conceptually simple but represents a creative solution to the problem of fuzzy clustering via hard clustering. However, novelty should not be conflated with validity: the approach's theoretical justification is weak, and empirical validation is compromised by methodological issues (circular evaluation, contradictory claims).
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If the RuThes results were corrected or explained (e.g., if WATSET actually outperformed baselines on RuThes with a different configuration), the main claim would be valid and the contribution would be stronger.
If formal justification were provided for why hard clustering on G' produces valid fuzzy clustering of G, the theoretical contribution would be solid.
If ablation studies showed that the hub effect reduction is the primary driver of performance improvement, the mechanism would be validated.
If the method were tested on additional under-resourced languages (beyond English and Russian), the cross-linguistic robustness claim would be credible.
If statistical significance tests showed that performance differences are meaningful despite low absolute F-scores, the empirical validation would be stronger.
If the circular evaluation on YARN were corrected (e.g., by using a held-out subset), the evaluation would be more rigorous.
If the proposed extension using distributional models were implemented and evaluated, the paper would address the acknowledged limitation of input dictionary completeness.

confidence_interval.rationale: The paper presents a novel and intuitive methodological contribution with comprehensive multi-lingual evaluation. However, critical methodological flaws significantly undermine confidence: (1) the main claim of outperformance on all four datasets is contradicted by RuThes results; (2) circular evaluation on YARN inflates performance metrics; (3) the theoretical justification for fuzzy clustering via hard clustering is lacking; (4) hub effect reduction is asserted but not quantified; (5) low absolute F-scores raise questions about task difficulty and evaluation appropriateness. These issues are not minor oversights but fundamental problems that affect the validity of the main claims. The paper would benefit from substantial revisions to address these concerns. The lower bound (0.55) reflects the severity of the contradictory RuThes results and circular evaluation; the upper bound (0.75) reflects the paper's clear presentation, comprehensive evaluation, and practical resource contribution.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper proposes WATSET, a meta-algorithm for synset induction that combines local word sense induction (WSI) via ego network clustering with global hard clustering on a disambiguated graph. The core methodological contribution is the insight that splitting polysemous nodes into sense nodes before global clustering can achieve fuzzy clustering using efficient hard clustering algorithms. The paper is empirically rigorous in scope (4 gold standards, 2 languages, 5 baselines, 3 edge weighting schemes) but exhibits critical validity concerns: (1) the main claim of outperformance on all four datasets is contradicted by RuThes results where WATSET underperforms MCL and MaxMax; (2) absolute F-scores are uniformly low (max 0.428), raising questions about practical utility; (3) key assumptions about word sense induction quality, embedding reliability, and the validity of the hard-to-fuzzy clustering mapping are not empirically validated; (4) the 150-word cluster pruning threshold is arbitrary and not justified; (5) circular evaluation on YARN inflates performance metrics; (6) no ablation studies isolate component contributions. The paper's strengths lie in its novel algorithmic framing, multi-lingual evaluation, and systematic comparison of edge weighting strategies. However, reproducibility is compromised by missing hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, lack of statistical significance testing, and incomplete documentation of implementation details.
logical_argument_graph: Premise 1: Synsets are cliques in a synonymy graph (A1, explicit assumption)
Premise 2: Hard clustering on an ambiguous graph fails for polysemous words (Section 3, motivation)
Premise 3: Word sense induction can split polysemous nodes into sense nodes (Section 3.3, operational assumption A3)
Premise 4: Cosine similarity between sense contexts reliably disambiguates neighbors (A4, implicit assumption)
Premise 5: Hard clustering on the disambiguated graph G' produces valid fuzzy clustering of G (A5, operational assumption)
Conclusion 1: WATSET meta-algorithm effectively performs fuzzy clustering (C1, main claim)
Premise 6: Disambiguation reduces hub effects linking unrelated nodes (Section 5.2, mechanism claim C2)
Conclusion 2: WATSET outperforms five baselines on F-score across four datasets (C3, empirical claim)
Uncertainty: RuThes results contradict C3 (WATSET F=0.139 vs MCL F=0.152, MaxMax F=0.164)
Premise 7: Embedding-based edge weighting (sim) outperforms binary/frequency weighting (Figure 3, C4)
Uncertainty: C4 qualified by MaxMax exception and Russian dataset inconsistency
Premise 8: WATSET requires no English pivot resource unlike BabelNet/UBY (C5, architectural claim)
Uncertainty: C5 not empirically validated; requires language-specific embeddings as alternative dependency
Premise 9: Method generalizes across resource-rich (English) and under-resourced (Russian) languages (C6)
Uncertainty: Russian input dictionary is larger than English (202K vs 71K synonyms), contradicting 'under-resourced' characterization
Chaining issue: Low absolute F-scores across all methods suggest task difficulty or evaluation setup problems, undermining interpretation of relative performance claims

concerns.title: Contradictory empirical claim on RuThes dataset
concerns.description: The abstract and main text claim WATSET outperforms all five baselines on all four datasets. However, Table 4 shows WATSET[CWlog, MCL] achieves F-score 0.139 on RuThes, which is lower than MCL (0.152) and MaxMax (0.164). This directly contradicts the main claim and undermines the paper's central empirical contribution.

Table 4 RuThes row: WATSET F=0.139, MCL F=0.152, MaxMax F=0.164
Section 5.2 does not acknowledge this contradiction
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Revise abstract and claims to accurately reflect results: WATSET wins on 3 of 4 datasets (WordNet, BabelNet, YARN) but underperforms on RuThes. Provide analysis of why RuThes is different (domain-specific vocabulary, different gold standard construction) and discuss implications for method robustness.

concerns.title: Uniformly low absolute F-scores raise questions about task difficulty and evaluation setup
concerns.description: Maximum F-score across all methods and datasets is 0.428 (YARN), with most results in the 0.1-0.3 range. Such low absolute performance raises fundamental questions about whether the task is well-defined, whether the evaluation metric is appropriate, or whether the method is practically useful. The paper does not adequately address this concern.
evidence: Table 3: English F-scores range from 0.136 to 0.374
Table 4: Russian F-scores range from 0.042 to 0.428
Section 6 acknowledges low performance on RuThes but attributes it to input dictionary coverage, not task difficulty
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze the source of low F-scores: (1) Is the F-score metric on binary pairs appropriate for evaluating synset quality? (2) Are gold standards incomplete or noisy? (3) Is the task inherently difficult? (4) Provide analysis of what F-score thresholds would be considered 'good' performance. Consider alternative evaluation metrics (e.g., cluster coherence, semantic meaningfulness) to complement F-score.

concerns.title: Arbitrary cluster size threshold of 150 words lacks empirical justification
concerns.description: The paper prunes clusters larger than 150 words as 'they hardly can represent any meaningful synset' (Section 5). This threshold appears arbitrary and is not empirically justified. The choice significantly impacts results (acknowledged for MaxMax and CPM) but is not systematically analyzed.
evidence: Section 5: 'we delete the clusters equal or larger than the threshold of 150 words'
Section 5.2: 'Without this pruning, the MaxMax and CPM methods tend to discover giant components obtaining almost zero precision'
No sensitivity analysis of threshold value provided
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct sensitivity analysis: vary the threshold (e.g., 50, 100, 150, 200, 300 words) and report how results change for each method. Provide empirical justification for the 150-word choice (e.g., analysis of gold standard synset size distribution). Alternatively, use a data-driven threshold based on gold standard statistics.

concerns.title: No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals
concerns.description: The paper reports point estimates of F-score, precision, and recall but provides no statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or multiple runs to assess variance. This makes it impossible to determine whether observed differences between methods are statistically meaningful.
evidence: Tables 3-4 report single F-score values with no error bars or significance indicators
No mention of multiple runs or cross-validation
No discussion of variance or stability of results
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run each method multiple times (if stochastic) or with different random seeds. Report mean and standard deviation of F-score. Conduct paired significance tests (e.g., McNemar's test for binary predictions) to determine whether WATSET's improvements over baselines are statistically significant at p<0.05.

concerns.title: Circular evaluation on YARN dataset inflates performance metrics
concerns.description: The paper uses the same input synonymy dictionary for both method input and YARN gold standard construction (Section 4.4). This introduces circularity: the method is evaluated on how well it recovers synsets built from the same raw materials it uses as input. Results on YARN are therefore not directly comparable to other datasets and likely overestimate method performance.
evidence: Section 4.4: 'the same input synonymy dictionary was used by authors of YARN to construct synsets using crowdsourcing'

Paper acknowledges this but does not correct for it: 'results on the YARN dataset show how close an automatic synset induction method can approximate manually created synsets provided the same starting raw linguistic materials'
YARN F-score (0.428) is highest among all datasets, suggesting inflation
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clearly flag YARN results as having potential circularity bias. Conduct separate evaluation on a held-out portion of YARN not used in input dictionary construction. Alternatively, use a different Russian gold standard (e.g., RuThes only) for primary evaluation. Discuss implications of circularity for interpreting results.

concerns.title: Missing ablation studies isolating component contributions
concerns.description: The paper does not provide ablation studies isolating the contributions of individual components: (1) word sense induction step, (2) disambiguation step, (3) global clustering algorithm choice, (4) edge weighting scheme. Without ablations, it is unclear which components drive performance and whether all five steps are necessary.
evidence: Section 3 describes five steps but no ablation study is provided
Section 5.1 analyzes edge weighting but not other components
No comparison of WATSET vs plain MCL on disambiguated graph to isolate WSI contribution
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide ablation studies: (1) WATSET vs plain MCL on original graph (to show WSI benefit), (2) WATSET vs MCL on disambiguated graph without WSI (to isolate disambiguation benefit), (3) WATSET with different WSI algorithms (CW vs MCL), (4) WATSET with different global clustering algorithms. Report F-score for each ablation to quantify component contributions.

concerns.title: Word sense induction quality not validated
concerns.description: The paper assumes that ego network clustering reliably separates word senses (Section 3.3, A3). However, no evaluation of WSI quality is provided. The use of 'hopefully' in Section 3.3 signals author uncertainty. For words with subtle sense distinctions or rare senses, ego network clustering may fail, propagating errors to downstream steps.
evidence: Section 3.3: 'each cluster is hopefully representing a different sense of the word u'
No evaluation of WSI accuracy (e.g., comparison to gold standard word senses)
No analysis of failure cases where WSI produces incorrect sense splits
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate WSI quality on a subset of words with known sense inventories (e.g., from WordNet). Report precision and recall of induced senses vs gold standard. Analyze failure cases: which words have poor sense induction? How does WSI quality correlate with final synset quality? Consider alternative WSI methods if current approach is unreliable.

concerns.title: Disambiguation accuracy not evaluated
concerns.description: The paper assumes that cosine similarity between sense contexts reliably disambiguates neighboring words (Section 3.4, A4). However, no evaluation of disambiguation accuracy is provided. If context vectors are noisy or if multiple senses have similar contexts, disambiguation will be incorrect, leading to spurious edges in the disambiguated graph G'.
evidence: Section 3.4 describes disambiguation approach but provides no accuracy evaluation
No analysis of when disambiguation fails or produces incorrect sense assignments
No comparison of disambiguation accuracy across different embedding models
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate disambiguation accuracy on a sample of words with known sense assignments. For each word in a sense context, check whether the disambiguated sense matches the gold standard sense. Report precision and recall of disambiguation. Analyze failure cases and their impact on final synset quality.

concerns.title: Embedding quality and alignment with synonymy not validated
concerns.description: The method relies on word embeddings for edge weighting (Section 3.2) and sense context representation (Section 3.4). However, embedding quality and alignment with synonymy relations are not validated. Poor embeddings could undermine the entire approach.

No analysis of whether embedding similarity correlates with true synonymy
No comparison of different embedding models (e.g., Word2Vec vs GloVe vs FastText)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Validate embedding quality: (1) Compute correlation between embedding cosine similarity and gold standard synonymy judgments. (2) Compare performance with different embedding models. (3) Analyze failure cases where embedding similarity contradicts true synonymy. (4) Discuss implications of embedding quality for method robustness.

concerns.title: Different WATSET configurations used for different datasets complicates interpretation
concerns.description: The paper uses different WATSET configurations for different datasets: WATSET[MCL, MCL] for English, WATSET[CWlog, MCL] for Russian. This makes it unclear which design choices matter and whether the method is robust to configuration choices.

Table 4: WATSET[CWlog, MCL] for RuThes and YARN

concerns.title: Hub effect reduction mechanism not quantitatively validated
concerns.description: The paper claims that disambiguation reduces hub effects (C2, Section 5.2) but provides no quantitative measurement of hub effect magnitude before and after disambiguation. concerns.actionable_suggestion: Quantify hub effects: (1) Identify hub nodes (high-degree nodes) in the original graph. (2) Measure their connectivity to semantically unrelated nodes. (3) Repeat analysis on disambiguated graph. (4) Report reduction in spurious hub connections. (5) Correlate hub effect reduction with performance improvement to validate the mechanism.

concerns.title: Hyperparameter sensitivity not systematically analyzed

alternative_interpretations: The low absolute F-scores across all methods might indicate that F-score on binary pairs is not an appropriate metric for evaluating synset quality, rather than indicating poor method performance. Alternative metrics (cluster coherence, semantic meaningfulness) might show different results.

The RuThes underperformance might reflect domain-specific challenges (high proportion of multiword expressions, domain-specific vocabulary) rather than fundamental method limitations. WATSET might be better suited to general vocabulary than domain-specific vocabulary.

The precision-recall tradeoff on Russian datasets might reflect a deliberate design choice to optimize for precision (fewer, higher-quality synsets) rather than recall (more, lower-quality synsets). This could be appropriate for some applications.

The circular evaluation on YARN might not be problematic if the goal is to measure how well the method recovers manually-created synsets from the same raw materials. This is a valid evaluation scenario even if not directly comparable to other datasets.

The different WATSET configurations for different datasets might reflect appropriate adaptation to dataset characteristics rather than lack of robustness. Language-specific or dataset-specific tuning could be reasonable.

The hub effect reduction might be the actual mechanism of improvement, even without quantitative validation. The qualitative explanation and single example might be sufficient for a methodological paper.

The low performance on RuThes might be due to gold standard quality issues (domain-specific vocabulary, multiword expressions) rather than method limitations. Cross-evaluation with other Russian resources (Table 5) shows low agreement between gold standards.
